statement: The organising of the 705 rooms sorts into 197 kinds of doing (183 on the main tier, 14 rare), and no kind holds more than 7% of the 7,786 placed second-order themes. Half of those themes (51.1%) carry one kind; the rest carry two (25.3%) or three (23.6%). Themes about dealing with other rooms (borders, truces, alliances, help, restraint) carry the most kinds at once: 36.0% of them sit on one kind, against 54.1% of the others.
bound: One reader's placements of the 7,786 second-order themes, before any fresh reader tested the gates. The share of themes that need two or three kinds rises with the grain of the second-order theme: 70.4% sit on one kind at five concepts or fewer, 35 to 38% at six to twenty. The share therefore measures the A1 coders' cut as well as what the rooms did.
refuted_by: Fresh readers at stage B2, holding the gates, disagree on the primary kind in more than a third of the second-order themes they place; or merging the dealing kinds (T3-010 with T3-149, T3-150 and T3-151) loses no distinction those readers draw.

bound: One reader's placements of the 7,786 second-order themes. Within a room, larger second-order themes carry more kinds (mean within-room Spearman 0.28 between a theme's concepts and its kinds, positive in 482 of 619 rooms; themes of five concepts or fewer sit on one kind 16 points above their room's own share). Across rooms, a room's grain predicts nothing (Spearman -0.08 between a room's mean concepts per theme and its single-kind share, 633 rooms). The B1e line said the share measures the A1 coders' cut and that grain separates canucks from turkey; that does not hold across rooms and is withdrawn.

why: the PI pointed out (2026-10-11, from the B1e interview) that the grain bound does not hold across rooms; b2_grain_check.py confirms it, and the bound is rewritten to the within-room relation the data show
